tldr: Vos argues kids should still learn to code in the AI era, and recounts how Devoxx4Kids Netherlands got Java to drive LEGO SPIKE robots through a Raspberry Pi bridge.
summary: Vos, chairman of the Devoxx4Kids Foundation in the Netherlands and an engineering manager at Ahold Delhaize, opens with the question parents, teachers and colleagues keep asking: why teach kids to code when AI writes it? His answer is the calculator analogy: we still teach that 7 times 8 is 56 so we can spot a machine saying 5600. AI can generate robot code, but judging it, spotting a loop that turns four times instead of three, or a motor that stalls on a slippery floor, takes understanding. Physical robots make bugs visible immediately, which keeps kids engaged.

LEGO SPIKE, the successor to Mindstorms, only supports blocks and Python, and its hub has about 320 KB of RAM, too little for a JVM. Using the protocol documentation LEGO publishes on GitHub, the team tried three routes: custom JVM firmware (rejected, as it could break schools' robots), Java generating MicroPython uploaded to a program slot (uploaded, but the robot did not move), and Java on a laptop over Bluetooth (no usable Java Bluetooth library on Windows). What worked was a simple Java API ('drive forward', 'turn right') talking to a Python bridge on a Raspberry Pi that speaks to the hub. The live demo eventually moved the robot; the distance sensor and non-blocking commands are still work in progress, and Vos asked for help. He credits Java 25's simple main methods with making Java approachable for ten-year-olds, and closes by asking Java developers to volunteer, host Devoxx4Kids days at their company or join the quarterly Dutch hackathons.
keyPoints: The SPIKE hub has around 320 KB of RAM, so a standard JVM cannot run on it, and flashing custom firmware would make school-owned robots unusable with LEGO's software.
Generating MicroPython from Java and uploading it to one of the hub's 20 program slots uploaded fine but did not make the robot move.
The working architecture is a Windows laptop running Java, a Raspberry Pi running a Python bridge, and the hub over Bluetooth; the goal is to drop the Pi now that a Java Bluetooth library exists.
SPIKE drive commands need both speed and duration, which the kid-facing Java API hides behind calls like drive-forward and turn-right.
Vos used AI to read LEGO's GitHub documentation and generate boilerplate, but found its byte-level output hard to trust and says API design for a ten-year-old still needs a human.
takeaways: Volunteer for a Devoxx4Kids workshop, or offer your company as a host for a Devoxx4Kids day.
When teaching beginners Java, use Java 25's simplified main method to remove the public static void boilerplate.
If you work with LEGO SPIKE, start from LEGO's published protocol documentation on GitHub and check the Devoxx4Kids repository before writing your own bridge.

quotes.text: AI changes how we write code, but not why we learn to code.
Prompting is asking, but building is understanding.
The developers from tomorrow are now 10 years old.

watchIf: You want to teach kids programming with robots or volunteer at Devoxx4Kids and want to see how Java can drive LEGO SPIKE hardware.
